claims.claim: Sadao Hasegawa's work, the review adds, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime.
claims.reason: The source says 'Most of the Japanese illustrator's work, you guessed it, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime.' The article drops 'most' and states it of his work as a whole, converting a partial claim into a total one. This matters because the article's closing argument leans on Hasegawa as a third case of work wholly unshown in a lifetime.

claims.claim: George never showed her work publicly in her lifetime and was found after 2013.
claims.reason: The source says she 'was only discovered after her death in 2013' — i.e. after her death, which occurred in 2013. 'Found after 2013' asserts a discovery date later than the year 2013, which the source does not establish; discovery could have happened within 2013. The article's own earlier paragraph states it correctly, so this is a drift introduced in the later restatement.

claims.claim: There is no map that resolves it.
claims.reason: The source establishes only the reviewer's experience — that EAF is 'big, unwieldy, confusing' and that 'it's impossible to figure out how any of it fits together'. It does not state that no orienting programme, guide or map exists. Stated flatly, this reads as a fact about the festival's provision rather than about the reviewer's experience of it. Resolving it would require evidence about EAF's actual visitor materials.

claims.claim: What it does not describe, and cannot, is the other span of time these dates measure: the years in which that same work went unshown while its maker was alive.
claims.reason: This is the article's own argument about what the word 'discovery' can and cannot denote, but 'cannot' states it as a settled property rather than as the article's reading. The source supports the underlying facts for George and Walter but not the generalisation across all three artists — for Hasegawa the source says only that 'most' of the work stayed unseen, so 'that same work went unshown' is not established for the full set the sentence gathers.

Pre-scan false positive. This is the article's own headline, not a named entity or factual claim; it is built directly on the source's 'You've just got to follow your nose' and the source's Edinburgh setting. Nothing is invented.

Pre-scan false positive on the name itself: 'Sadao Hasegawa (1945-1999)' appears verbatim in the source, along with Custom Lane as his venue. The pre-scan matched on the possessive form. The genuine problem in that sentence is the dropped quantifier, flagged separately above.
